metadata.title: Cervical spine clearance in the trauma patient
quality_flags: The imaging scenario table appears after the heading for standard 8, although standard 7 refers to its scenarios.
Reference 2 is cited but absent from the reference list.
metadata.summary: This standard sets out clinical and imaging criteria for clearing the cervical spine in adults after blunt trauma. It addresses when spinal protection can be withdrawn, when it must continue, and when specialist referral or MRI is needed.

care_settings: centres capable of emergency spinal surgery
target_population: adults who have sustained blunt trauma

prophylaxis.recommendation: Hospitals treating trauma patients must have a spinal protection protocol. Spinal protection must continue when an injury is identified or until injury is excluded through an established protocol. Early formal spinal precautions are often necessary, but maintaining them for more than 48 hours is not recommended because of the need for log rolling and complications such as pressure sores.
prophylaxis.target_population: Adult patients sustaining blunt trauma when spinal injury is suspected or identified.
prophylaxis.duration: Until injury is excluded through an established protocol; continuation for more than 48 hours is not recommended.

therapies_index.administration: Early formal precautions are often necessary; continuation for more than 48 hours is not recommended. They may be removed after qualifying radiological clearance, although clinical clearance requires a documented tertiary survey.

therapies_index.administration: Required when spinal precautions are continued.

conditions.name: cervical spine injury
conditions.description: After blunt trauma, cervical spine injury may compromise spinal stability. An injury can be occult when it involves disc or ligamentous disruption.

subtypes.name: occult cervical spine injury
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May involve disruption of a disc or ligament.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In an awake and orientated patient; also after an inconclusive CT once the patient is fully conscious.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A normal examination in an awake and orientated patient excludes significant spinal injury. After an inconclusive CT, protection continues until MRI is performed or a normal examination is documented in a fully conscious patient.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify suspected spinal injury and document the findings.
Document neurological findings on an agreed proforma, such as an ASIA chart.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When abnormal clinical signs are present.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Neurological abnormalities consistent with spinal cord injury require immediate discussion with, and referral to, a centre capable of emergency spinal surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess these spinal regions according to major trauma protocols.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As specified by major trauma protocols.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the cervical spine for injury and signs of instability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Without delay when cervical spine injury is suspected; imaging protocols are also needed to exclude significant spinal injury in unconscious or uncooperative patients and those with significant distracting injuries.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Thin-slice imaging must extend from the occiput to T4 and include sagittal and coronal reconstructions. An injury that could affect stability calls for continued spinal protection and advice from an appropriate clinical team. A good-quality scan without interpretation-confounding comorbidities or signs of instability, such as fracture, haematoma or joint disruption, permits radiological clearance and removal of precautions in an unconscious or obtunded patient; clinical clearance still requires a completed and documented tertiary survey. If scan quality is inadequate or comorbidities hinder interpretation, protection continues until MRI or a documented normal clinical examination in a fully conscious patient. An initial imaging report should be available before departure from the Emergency Department and a definitive report within 18 hours of injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Include assessment of the cervical spine when injury is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When whole-body trauma imaging is necessary and cervical spine injury is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Include the cervical spine in imaging performed for head injury.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When brain CT is needed for head injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess a suspected cord injury, an ambiguous CT, an ankylosed spine with negative or indeterminate CT findings for fracture, or a patient with a contraindication to ionising radiation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When any of these circumstances is present, including pregnancy as an example of a contraindication to ionising radiation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Complete and document clinical clearance after radiological clearance.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After spinal precautions are removed on the basis of qualifying CT findings in an unconscious or obtunded patient.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Radiological clearance alone does not establish clinical clearance.

rows: Every hospital treating trauma patients must have a spinal protection protocol.
Maintain spinal protection when an injury is identified, or until an established protocol excludes injury.
When injury is suspected, assess the entire spine and document the findings.
If clinical signs are abnormal, perform and document a complete neurological examination using an agreed proforma, such as an ASIA chart.
If abnormal neurological findings are consistent with spinal cord injury, immediately discuss the case with and refer the patient to a centre able to perform emergency spinal surgery.
6a
Significant spinal injury is excluded by a normal clinical examination in an awake, orientated patient.
6b
For an unconscious or uncooperative patient, or one with significant distracting injuries, significant spinal injury is excluded after completion of the imaging protocol in standard 7.
7a
Obtain thoracic and lumbar spine scans in accordance with major trauma protocols.
7b
When cervical spine injury is suspected, promptly obtain thin slice CT from the occiput to T4, with sagittal and coronal reconstructions.
7c
When trauma requires whole-body CT (WBCT), include the cervical spine if injury is suspected.
7d
When head injury requires brain CT, include the cervical spine.
7e

Make an initial cervical spine clearance imaging report available before departure from the Emergency Department and a definitive report within 18 hours of injury; the report should identify one of the scenarios and actions in the accompanying table.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging is necessary for suspected cord injury; ambiguous CT findings as described in option 3 of standard 7; an ankylosed spine when CT findings for fracture are negative or indeterminate; or a contraindication to ionising radiation, for example pregnancy.

artifacts.summary: The numbered standards set out requirements for spinal protection, examination, referral, imaging and clearance after blunt trauma. They also specify when Magnetic Resonance Imaging is necessary.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The checklist helps clinicians determine which assessments and imaging must precede removal of spinal protection, and when urgent specialist referral is required.

recommendations.statement: Every hospital that manages trauma patients must have a spinal protection protocol.
Maintain spinal protection when an injury is identified, or until an established protocol excludes injury.
When spinal injury is suspected, assess the entire spine and document the findings.
If clinical signs are abnormal, perform and document a complete neurological examination using an agreed proforma, such as an ASIA chart.
If abnormal neurological signs are consistent with spinal cord injury, immediately discuss the patient with, and refer the patient to, a centre able to perform emergency spinal surgery.
A normal clinical examination in a patient who is awake and orientated excludes significant spinal injury.
recommendations.context: Clinical criterion for excluding significant spinal injury.

recommendations.statement: For unconscious or uncooperative patients, and for patients with significant distracting injuries, exclude significant spinal injury by completing the spinal imaging protocols in standard 7.
recommendations.context: Imaging criterion for excluding significant spinal injury.

recommendations.statement: Obtain thoracic and lumbar spine scans in accordance with major trauma protocols.
When cervical spine injury is suspected, promptly perform thin slice CT from the occiput to T4, with sagittal and coronal reconstructions.
When trauma requires whole-body CT (WBCT), include the cervical spine if injury is suspected.
When a head injury requires brain CT, include the cervical spine.
Make an initial report of cervical spine clearance imaging available before the patient leaves the Emergency Department, and provide a definitive report within 18 hours of injury.
recommendations.context: The definitive report should identify the applicable imaging scenario and action.

recommendations.statement: If cervical spine clearance imaging identifies an injury that could compromise spinal stability, maintain spinal protection and obtain advice from an appropriate clinical team.

If the scan is of good quality, no comorbidities complicate its interpretation, and it shows no indicators of instability such as fracture, haematoma or joint disruption, an unconscious or obtunded patient may be designated “C-Spine radiologically cleared” and spinal precautions may be removed. Clinical clearance remains unconfirmed until a tertiary survey has been completed and documented.

If CT shows no clear signs of spinal instability but is of inadequate quality and/or its interpretation is complicated by comorbidities, continue spinal protection until MRI is performed or the patient is fully conscious and a normal clinical examination is documented.
Perform Magnetic Resonance Imaging when cord injury is suspected.
Perform Magnetic Resonance Imaging for an ambiguous CT scan, as described in option 3 of standard 7.
Perform Magnetic Resonance Imaging for an ankylosed spine when CT findings for fracture are negative or indeterminate.
Perform Magnetic Resonance Imaging when ionising radiation is contraindicated, for example during pregnancy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adult patients after blunt trauma in whom a cervical spine injury is suspected.
decision_rules: Apply the hospital's spinal protection protocol while an injury remains possible; maintain protection if an injury is identified or until an established protocol excludes it.
Assess and document the entire spine when injury is suspected.
Obtain thoracic and lumbar spine scans in accordance with major trauma protocols.
If cervical spine injury is suspected, perform thin slice CT from occiput to T4 with sagittal and coronal reconstructions without delay.
Include the cervical spine when whole-body CT (WBCT) is needed for trauma and cervical injury is suspected, or when brain CT is needed for head injury.

document_sections.heading: Background and justification
document_sections.content: After blunt trauma, particularly when cognition is impaired, an unstable cervical spine is a recognised possibility and patients are protected accordingly. Formal spinal precautions are often needed early, but their continuation for more than 48 hours is not recommended because log rolling is required and complications, including pressure sores, can occur. Cervical spine injury involving a disc or ligament may be occult. The guideline sets out an early clinical and radiological pathway for deciding when to withdraw full spine precautions from patients initially suspected of cervical spine injury.

document_sections.heading: Inclusions:
document_sections.content: The guideline applies to adult patients who have sustained blunt trauma.

document_sections.heading: Standards
document_sections.content: Every hospital that manages trauma patients must have a spinal protection protocol. Spinal protection must continue when an injury is found and otherwise must remain until an established protocol excludes injury. When spinal injury is suspected, the entire spine should be assessed and the findings documented. Abnormal clinical signs require a complete neurological examination, recorded on an agreed proforma such as an ASIA chart. Neurological abnormalities consistent with spinal cord injury require immediate discussion with, and referral to, a centre able to perform emergency spinal surgery. Significant spinal injury is excluded by a normal clinical examination in an awake, orientated patient, or by completion of the imaging protocols in a patient who is unconscious or uncooperative or has significant distracting injuries. Thoracic and lumbar scans should follow major trauma protocols. Suspected cervical spine injury calls for thin slice CT from the occiput to T4, with sagittal and coronal reconstructions, without delay. When trauma requires whole-body CT (WBCT), the scan should include the cervical spine if injury is suspected; CT needed for head injury should also include the cervical spine. An initial report of imaging used for cervical spine clearance should be available before the patient leaves the Emergency Department, and a definitive report should be available within 18 hours of injury. The report should identify which of 3 scenarios applies and the corresponding action: an injury that may compromise spinal stability requires continued spinal protection and advice from an appropriate clinical team; a good-quality scan without comorbidities that hinder interpretation or signs of instability, such as fracture, haematoma or joint disruption, permits an unconscious or obtunded patient to be designated “C-Spine radiologically cleared” and spinal precautions to be removed, although clinical clearance remains unconfirmed until a tertiary survey is completed and documented; if no clear instability is seen but CT quality is inadequate and/or comorbidities hinder interpretation, spinal protection should continue until MRI is performed or the patient is fully conscious and a normal clinical examination is documented. Magnetic Resonance Imaging is necessary for suspected cord injury, ambiguous CT findings corresponding to the third scenario, an ankylosed spine with CT findings that are negative or indeterminate for fracture, or a contraindication to ionising radiation, for example pregnancy.
